Ok, I've finished the math on this.

Ceres temperature in sunlight gets up to 235K (-38C, -36F) according to wikipedia.

An ideal gas (which this isn't, but it'll serve our purpose as an estimate) has an velocity given by the formula

(1) E=1/2mv^2=f/2TR/N

(f is degrees of freedom (7 for an ideal triatomic gas), T is temperature, R is the universal gas constant, N is Avogadro's number, m is the molecular mass) simplifies to

(2) v=sqrt(fTR/m) (good news for sanity, molecular mass*N=mass in grams/mol, so N just sorta vanishes)

This works out to an average molecular velocity of 871m/s (I think the actual will be closer to 806, going by the gap between predicted and actual specific heat of water vapor at 225K). But the escape velocity on ceres is just 510m/s. Not every molecule will have that velocity all the time, but more than half of it at any given time will. So any water vapor at that temperature will rapidly escape its minuscule gravity well. The crater walls however make the gas bounce back off, only gas molecules with an upward direction get to escape, this will slow the loss of gas and allow some, if not very much, gas to remain trapped in the crater.
